name: Little CMS
baseline: babl (GIMP/GEGL pixel-format and colour conversion library)
workload: Author's throughput test program running the same colour transform through babl, stock lcms2 and lcms2 with the fast-float plugin, on a low-end machine (image size and profiles not visible in the snippet).
claimed_speedup: Stock lcms2 took 3.59 s against 6.36 s for babl (about 1.77x, the post calls it 77% faster); with the fast-float plugin 1.7 s (the post calls it a 273% boost over babl, about 3.7x; derived from page data).
hardware: low-end machine, CPU model not stated in the snippet
stars_or_usage: 753 stars; shipped in most Linux distributions, used in GIMP, Ghostscript, MuPDF and many others per the README
tradeoffs: Core library is MIT. The fast-float plugin (plugins/fast_float, floating-point pipelines, 8/15/16-bit optimised paths) and the threaded plugin are GPL-3.0 and the plugin PDF says a commercial licence is available for a fee, so the 3.7x figure is not available under the MIT licence. Plugin trades a small accuracy epsilon for speed (testbed allows EPSILON_FLOAT_TESTS).
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: littlecms.com is blocked by the egress proxy in this session, so the numbers come from a WebSearch result summary of the blog post, not from the page itself; wording ('77% faster', '273% boost') is the search summary's paraphrase and may differ from the post. First-party (the library author), written in reply to the GIMP 2.10 release notes claiming babl is up to 10 times faster than lcms2, so the claim is contested by the baseline's own project. One test machine, no compiler flags, image size, profile pair or CPU model visible. The repo carries the benchmark harness (plugins/fast_float/testbed/fast_float_testbed.c has SpeedTest8bitsRGB etc. printing MPixel/sec) but it compares fast_float against stock lcms2 and no results are checked into the repo. Little CMS's README and doc PDFs (2.19 tutorial and API) contain no benchmark numbers at all. A third-party README (jsColorEngine) reports a native lcms2 2.18 matrix-shaper RGB to RGB path about 1.4x faster than its own WASM-SIMD kernel, but its author says those native numbers are being re-measured, so it was not used.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-c Graphics list entry (https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c#Graphics); WebSearch 'littlecms.com blog Babl throughput comparative' surfaced https://littlecms.com/blog/2019/10/02/througput-babl/; repo page https://github.com/mm2/Little-CMS and plugins/fast_float opened

name: MuPDF
workload: py-pdf/benchmarks: wall-clock time to extract the text of 14 pure (non-scanned) PDFs, and to extract their images, driven from Python through PyMuPDF (MuPDF), pdftotext (poppler) and pypdfium2 (PDFium).
claimed_speedup: Text extraction average 0.1 s for PyMuPDF against 0.3 s for pdftotext (poppler); per document 0.3 s against 1.0 s (GeoTopo-book) and 0.2 s against 0.8 s (1707.09725); pypdfium2 (PDFium) ties PyMuPDF at 0.1 s average. Image extraction average 0.5 s for PyMuPDF against 1.0 s for pypdfium2 (about 2x, derived from page data); poppler is not in the image row.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (PyMuPDF and pypdfium2 are prebuilt PyPI wheels, versions 1.28.2 and 5.13.0; pdftotext 0.86.1 built against the system libpoppler-cpp-dev)
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars on the GitHub mirror; backs PyMuPDF and is embedded in many viewers and tools
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 (commercial licence from Artifex for closed-source use), so copyleft applies to network services and products. The py-pdf numbers were taken through the PyMuPDF Python binding and pdftotext's Python binding, so both include Python call and string-copy overhead.
caveats: Independent suite (py-pdf organisation, BSD-3-Clause, runs the same script for every library; code public) but compiler and flags are not stated, so it is B not A. Times are rounded to 0.1 s, which makes the 0.1 s versus 0.3 s average coarse. The measured jobs are text and image extraction (parsing and interpreting content streams), not page rasterisation, so category rasterizers-2d is a best fit; the orchestrator may prefer a document-parsing category. First-party rendering evidence also exists: PyMuPDF docs Appendix 4 (https://github.com/pymupdf/PyMuPDF/blob/main/docs/app4.rst) report 150 DPI page rendering totals of 367.04 s for PyMuPDF against 646 s for XPDF pdftopng (rate 1.76) and 851.52 s for PDF2JPG across eight Artifex sample PDFs, and plain text extraction 8.01 s against 27.42 s for XPDF (3.42x); that page states no CPU or compiler and XPDF is poppler's ancestor rather than poppler, so it is tier C and was not used as the headline. PDF Association survey (pdfa.org, 2021) and an Alfresco blog compare MuPDF, poppler and PDFium rendering but both hosts are blocked here, so their figures were not read. Bindings (PyMuPDF, pypdfium2) are what the suite times, not the C libraries directly.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-cpp PDF list entry (https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#PDF); WebSearch 'MuPDF faster than poppler pdfium rendering benchmark pages per second' led to PyMuPDF docs and the py-pdf/benchmarks README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
